title: Sourdough crumb structure, open versus tight
subtitle: What determines the size of the holes and how to target the crumb you want
excerpt: The crumb structure of sourdough bread, the pattern and size of holes inside the loaf, is determined by hydration, fermentation time, folding technique, and shaping. An open crumb has large, irregular holes; a tight crumb is fine and uniform. Neither is better; both are the right result for the right bread.
sourceNotes: Crumb structure in sourdough is determined by fermentation, hydration, and shaping, as established in practical sourdough baking literature. The relationship between these variables and the resulting crumb is well-documented.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sourdough crumb with large, irregular holes and thin cell walls. Associated with high hydration, full fermentation, gentle handling, and minimal degassing during shaping. Typical of country loaves and ciabatta.
A sourdough crumb with small, even holes and thicker cell walls. Associated with lower hydration, more vigorous shaping, or a sandwich loaf dough that needs to hold filling without collapsing.
The gas bubbles in a fermented dough that become the holes in the crumb after baking. Larger, more numerous alveoli produce an open crumb; smaller, fewer alveoli produce a tighter crumb.

High hydration (75% and above): wetter doughs ferment more quickly and the gas bubbles are larger. Gentle handling: every fold, shape, or knock-back pops gas bubbles; the more careful the handling, the more gas is preserved. Full bulk fermentation: a dough that has fully fermented has more gas to distribute. Cold retard: extends the time gas can accumulate before the surface of the loaf sets.

Lower hydration (65% and below): denser doughs produce smaller, more evenly distributed bubbles. Vigorous shaping: tight shaping degasses the dough and compresses the bubbles. Sandwich loaf formulas: enriched doughs with oil, butter, or milk are specifically designed for a fine, even crumb that slices cleanly and holds a filling.
Why the crumb comes out wrong

Dense crumb with no holes: underfermentation, too much degassing during shaping, or overproofing that collapses the structure before baking. Gummy crumb (holes but sticky): cut too soon after baking, or the loaf was slightly undercooked. The crumb sets as it cools, leaving a loaf at least 1 hour before cutting allows the starch to gelatinise fully.

attrs.title: The crumb is not the only measure

content.text: Instagram sourdough culture prizes extremely open crumbs. For most eating purposes, a medium-open crumb in a country loaf that slices well and toasts evenly is more useful than the most dramatic holes. Aim for the crumb the recipe specifies, not the one that photographs best.
